body:
The maintainer raised the priority from P8 to P4 (2026-11-18). His words:

> the issues of using gpu shaders for different things should be prioritized..

The issue stays `needs-research`. An agent works the research in the research lane (no branch, no PR, no lane slot) and files the sub-issues. The agent sets each sub-issue to P4 while the maintainer's order stands.
claimed: coordinator research agent (Opus) · 2026-11-18T21:50Z · worktree/branch none · plan: research

## Research 1/4: what exists today, and the candidates

All paths and lines are at `origin/main` 1613e42f9.

### GPU stack today
- wgpu `30.0.1`, naga `30.0.1`, egui-wgpu `=0.36.2` (`Cargo.lock`). There is no direct wgpu dependency. `camcraft-ui` uses the `egui_wgpu::wgpu` re-export (`Cargo.toml` lines 46-47, `crates/ui/Cargo.toml` lines 19-23).
- Only `camcraft-ui` links wgpu. `camcraft-app`, `camcraft-motion`, `camcraft-sim` and the CLI/MCP have no GPU access.
- Backends: the viewport tries the preferred backend, then `Backends::PRIMARY` (Vulkan, Metal, DX12, WebGPU), then `Backends::all()` (GL too) (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/gpu.rs` lines 94-102). The browser build accepts WebGPU or WebGL2 (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell_web.rs` line 86).
- One compute shader exists: the stock preview march, M7.2 B (`crates/ui/src/trace.rs`, 342 lines; `crates/ui/src/trace.wgsl`, 219 lines). It is display only. It has a CPU twin (`trace/cpu_eye.rs`) and a parity suite (`crates/ui/tests/trace_parity.rs`). A device that refuses the kernel, or a lattice past `max_storage_buffer_binding_size`, gives `Err` and the CPU march runs (`trace.rs` lines 1-25, 170, 271; `trace/eye.rs` lines 9-13).
- A headless device exists: `crates/ui/src/headless_gpu.rs` (software adapter first, then hardware; loud SKIP with no adapter; `CAMCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1` makes a missing adapter a failure, lines 1-100).
- No toolpath generator, gouge check or rest calculation uses the GPU.

### Where the candidate work runs now (all CPU, f64)
| Step | Code | Cost driver |
|---|---|---|
| 3D finishing drop-cutter (ball support height) | `crates/motion/src/finishing3d/support.rs`: `build_sups` 27-50, `ball_clear` 132-142, `column_clear` 162, `support_at` 368-388; walked by `march.rs` `march_curve` 44-305 from `raster.rs` `raster_pass` | Linear scan of ALL facets for each sample (padded box reject only), and `ball_clear` scans all facets again for each candidate. There is no spatial index. Cost is about samples x facets. |
| Facet gouge law (verify) | `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/gouge.rs` `facet_gouge` 43-172, `dist_seg_tri` 174 | Segment x triangle exact distances. Facets are already put in XY bins (lines 65-131). |
| 2D offsets (pocket, contour, adaptive rings) | `crates/geometry/src/geo2d.rs` `Region::offset` 373-390, `offset_sharp` 392; Clipper2 port on i64 at `SCALE = 1e6` (1 nm, line 26) | Exact integer polygon offsets. Already deterministic. |
| 2D rest material | `crates/motion/src/machining2d/rest2d.rs` (morphological opening by offsets, lines 1-25) | Two offsets and one difference. |
| Adaptive in-process stock | `crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive/raster.rs` (bitmap: `from_region` 37, `cut` 131, `engage` 165); `raster/conservative.rs` | Many small queries inside the planner loop, one at a time. |
| 3D rough islands and rest | `crates/motion/src/machining3d/rest.rs` `material_above` 47, `level_target` 56; `machining3d/hsm.rs` lines 1-23 | Plane slices of the model for each level. |
| Stock simulation | `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/` (column engine `dexel*.rs`, brick SDF `field*.rs`, seam `backend.rs`) | CPU. Display picture only on the GPU (above). |

Parallelism: `crates/app/src/commands/operation/generate.rs` line 281 runs the operations in parallel with rayon. Inside one operation the raster lines run on one thread.

### Candidates, by fit to the GPU
1. **Drop-cutter height field** (inverse tool offset on a grid): good fit. Many independent samples over one read-only facet set. Published: M. Inui, "Fast inverse offset computation using polygon rendering hardware", Computer-Aided Design 35(2), 2003, 191-201; M. Inui et al., "Using a GPU to accelerate die and mold fabrication", IEEE CG&A 27(1), 2007, 82-88. The depth buffer acts as a Z-map (B. K. Choi and R. B. Jerard, "Sculptured Surface Machining", Kluwer 1998, for the Z-map model).
2. **Gouge check first filter**: good fit. Many independent segment-facet pairs.
3. **2D offsets by distance field**: poor fit. The exact i64 Clipper2 result is better than any grid. The 2D rest material comes from these offsets, so it is a poor fit too.
4. **Adaptive in-process stock bitmap**: poor fit. The planner asks small serial questions. One GPU round trip (submit, map, read back) costs more than the CPU answer.
5. **3D rest from the stock field**: this is stock simulation work (the M7.3 family and #2607). It is not part of this issue.

A first finding without a GPU: the drop-cutter has no spatial index. A CPU grid of facets removes most of the cost. It also gives the CPU reference that a GPU result must match. See comment 3/4.

## Research 2/4: accuracy, the Prime Directive and determinism

### Precision of the GPU
- WGSL core has `f32` only. It has no `f64` type. wgpu has `Features::SHADER_F64`, but it is native only and not in WebGPU. Thus a portable kernel computes in f32.
- The WGSL specification (W3C, "Floating Point Accuracy") gives correct rounding for `+ - *` only. Division is 2.5 ULP. `inverseSqrt` is 2 ULP, and `sqrt` inherits its error from it. `fma` inherits the accuracy of `x * y + z`. The rounding mode is not specified. An implementation can flush denormals for the listed operations.
- f32 spacing at 500 mm is 2^-15 mm (about 0.00003 mm). Thus coordinates of a 500 mm part are not the problem. The problem is cancellation in the tangency and distance terms (for example `sqrt(r^2 - d^2)` near the rim of the ball). Tile-relative coordinates (vertex minus tile origin) keep the magnitudes small.

### Grid resolution against the tolerance
- A tolerance of 0.01 mm over 500 mm needs a 50 000 x 50 000 grid. That is 2.5e9 cells, or 10 GB in f32. This is far past `max_storage_buffer_binding_size` (WebGPU default 128 MiB). It needs tiles, and each tile needs one round trip.
- A grid does not know the height between its samples. A narrow rib or a sharp ridge between two samples is lost (the Z-map sampling error, Choi and Jerard 1998). Thus a grid value can never be the posted cutter height.

### Decision: the GPU only filters; the CPU f64 code decides
Recommended: **use the GPU only as a first filter before the exact CPU result.**
- The posted height stays the f64 answer of `support_at` (`support.rs` 368-388), at the true sample point.
- The GPU gives a conservative bound for each cell, with a margin larger than the f32 error bound. The CPU uses it only to skip facets that cannot be the support.
- `ball_clear` (`support.rs` 132-142) stays the certifier. It always runs in f64 against every facet near the ball (from a CPU grid, not from the GPU).
- Why this is safe: if the GPU bound is wrong and skips the true support facet, the CPU candidate is too low. The full `ball_clear` then finds the skipped facet inside the ball, and refuses that candidate. The result is a higher search or a refusal by name. It is never a gouge.
- The gouge check uses the same rule. The GPU marks the segment-bin pairs whose distance is below `r + margin`. The f64 `dist_seg_tri` (`gouge.rs` 174) measures each marked pair. An unmarked pair is a GPU miss only if the margin is wrong. To make this safe, the bin test stays a superset test and has a CPU parity test.
- Dropped: a GPU height field as the posted toolpath (option "use"). Reason: it breaks the tolerance between samples and the f64 path, and it would let a driver error reach the spindle.
- Dropped: f64 on the GPU (`SHADER_F64`). Reason: it is native only, Vulkan only in wgpu, and slow on most consumer GPUs.

### Determinism and goldens
- GPU results are not the same bits on all adapters. Division and `inverseSqrt` are not correctly rounded. Denormal flush is optional. The driver compilers can contract `a * b + c` into an FMA.
- With the filter design, no GPU value enters the output. The output is the f64 CPU value. Thus the CL file and the G-code are the same with the GPU on, with the GPU off, and on each adapter.
- Pinning test for each GPU slice: generate the same operation with the GPU filter on and off, and assert the same `.cl` and `.cnc` bytes against the existing goldens in `crates/app/tests/golden/`. Run it on the software adapter (lavapipe, WARP) and on hardware where present. A second test asserts that the GPU candidate set is a superset of the CPU candidate set.
- No new golden file is necessary for the GPU. A new golden would show a GPU dependency, which is the defect that the test must catch.

## Research 3/4: speed and transfer cost

The research ran no build and no benchmark (research lane rule). The numbers below are estimates from the code shape. Slices 1 and 3 must measure them on the large fixtures and put the readings in their PR bodies.

### Drop-cutter (3D finishing)
- Now: each sample of `support_at` tests every facet (box reject), and each accepted candidate calls `ball_clear`, which tests every facet again. For F facets and S samples the cost is about S x F box tests plus the exact tests. Example: F = 200 000 facets, S = 1 000 000 samples gives 2e11 box tests. That is minutes on one thread.
- CPU grid of facets (slice 1): each sample reads only the facets of its cell, typically tens. Example: 1e6 x 50 = 5e7 tests, about one second. The expected gain is two to three orders of magnitude. The output is the same bits, because the same f64 functions run on a subset that holds every facet that can touch the ball.
- Parallel raster lines on the CPU (rayon is in the tree, `crates/app/Cargo.toml` line 25): a further gain of about the core count. Order-preserving `collect` keeps the output the same (`crates/app/src/operation/job.rs` line 13 states this law).
- GPU filter on top (slice 3): it can remove most exact `tangent_z` calls. After slice 1 the remaining CPU work is small. Thus the GPU gain is estimated at 2x to 10x on very large meshes (1e6 facets and more), and small or negative on small parts.

### Transfer cost
- Upload: a facet is 9 f32 (36 bytes). 1e6 facets is 36 MB, about 3-10 ms over PCIe 3/4. The facet set is read-only for one operation, thus one upload for each generation.
- Readback: one f32 bound for each cell. A 4096 x 4096 tile is 64 MiB, about 5-10 ms. Readback needs a `map_async` wait (`crates/ui/src/trace/readback.rs`, native only).
- Fixed cost: device creation is 50-500 ms (driver dependent). It must be paid once for each process and cached, never for each operation.
- Integrated GPUs share main RAM, so the copy is cheaper, but compute is slower.

### Gouge check
- `facet_gouge` already bins facets (`gouge.rs` 65-131). A GPU pair filter gains only on very long programs against very large meshes. It is a later slice.

### Not worth the GPU
- 2D offsets: Clipper2 on i64 already answers in milliseconds for typical pockets, and exactly.
- Adaptive bitmap: one round trip (0.1-1 ms) for each planner question is slower than the CPU answer (microseconds).

Conclusion: the CPU spatial index is the first and largest gain. The GPU filter is a second gain for very large meshes. Both must give the same bytes.

## Research 4/4: platform, architecture, the simulation, recommendation and sub-issues

### Platform, no GPU, bad adapter
- Compute works on Vulkan, Metal, DX12 and WebGPU. It does not work on WebGL2, and not on GL below ES 3.1 (`DownlevelFlags::COMPUTE_SHADERS`). The viewport chain can land on GL (`gpu.rs` lines 99-100), so a compute probe is necessary.
- No adapter, a failed probe, a lost device or a buffer past the limit: **the CPU path runs, with the same result**. It is not a refusal. The log names the reason one time. Reason: the GPU only filters, so the CPU path is complete. A refusal would stop a user with a bad driver (#2424, #74) for no safety gain.
- A switch turns the GPU compute off (recommended `CAMCRAFT_GPU_COMPUTE=off`) for machines with bad drivers and for tests.
- Headless tests, the CLI and MCP: they use a windowless device (the `headless_gpu.rs` policy, moved to a lower crate). On a machine with no adapter, the CPU path runs. GPU suites follow #615: a loud SKIP, and `CAMCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1` makes the skip a failure. The self-hosted runners have the Mesa software drivers (`runners` skill), so lavapipe runs the GPU lanes there.
- Browser (#31): WebGPU only, with async readback. WebGL2 uses the CPU path. This is the last slice.

### Frame target
Generation runs in the generate job, never in a frame. The device is made once for each process and cached. The GPU result is made once for each operation generation. This obeys the rule "derived data is precalculated and cached, never per frame" (#2238).

### Architecture
- Recommended: a new crate for headless compute (name `camcraft-gpu`). It holds the device policy (moved from `crates/ui/src/headless_gpu.rs`), the capability probe, the kernels and their CPU-fallback contract.
- `camcraft-app` calls it in the generate job and passes the result into `camcraft-motion` and `camcraft-sim` as a value. Motion and sim get no GPU dependency. This follows "the caller passes the value in".
- New crate edges need a `docs/decisions/` entry (slice 2). A direct `wgpu` dependency is new for the workspace. It must be the version that the egui set pins (`=30.0.1`), so the lock gets no second wgpu. The review sets `needs-maintainer` for it.
- Dropped: kernels inside `camcraft-motion`. Reason: it would put wgpu into every motion build and test, and into the domain crate.
- Dropped: sharing the viewport's device. Reason: the CLI and MCP have no window, and a generation must not wait on the render queue.
- Commands: no new command. The GPU changes how fast a result comes, not what it is. Undo and the project file are not changed.

### Relation to the stock simulation
- The simulation uses the GPU only for the display picture (M7.2 B: `crates/ui/src/trace.rs`, `trace.wgsl`, `trace_parity.rs`). The verdicts and the post gate never read the GPU (`crates/sim/src/play_precalc.rs` lines 7-9 state "Display only").
- Shared with this work: the device policy, the refusal law ("the GPU is a speedup, never a dependency", `trace/eye.rs` lines 9-13), and the parity test pattern. Not shared: the kernels.
- GPU stock simulation is #2607. The 3D rest material from the stock field belongs there and to the M7.3 family, not here.

### Recommendation
**Use the GPU only as a first filter before an exact CPU f64 result.** Do not use it to make posted heights or offsets. Do not use it for 2D offsets, 2D rest material or the adaptive bitmap: the exact CPU paths are better there (comment 1/4 and 3/4).

### Sub-issues (all `P4` by the maintainer order of 2026-11-18, linked under this issue)
| Slice | Issue | Labels | Needs |

| 1 | #2619 3D finishing: CPU facet grid for the drop-cutter support scan | `effort:high`, `area:3d` | - |
| 2 | #2620 GPU compute seam crate, probe, CPU fallback, facet binning kernel | `effort:high`, `area:3d`, `area:build` | #2619 |
| 3 | #2621 GPU inverse-offset height bound as a filter for the f64 drop-cutter | `effort:max`, `area:3d` | #2619, #2620 |

| 5 | #2623 Browser build: GPU filter on WebGPU, CPU path on WebGL2 | `effort:high`, `area:ui`, `area:build` | #2621 |

Slice 1 is small and runs headless with no GPU. Each GPU slice names its CPU reference test: GPU on and GPU off give the same bytes.

### Not answered by this research
- Measured speed. The research lane runs no build. Slices 1 and 3 measure on the large fixtures and report in their PR bodies. If the GPU filter gives no gain, slice 3 keeps the switch off by default.

All questions of this issue have answers in comments 1/4 to 4/4. This research is complete. The issue closes now, by the `needs-research` procedure.
Research complete. Sub-issues: #2619, #2620, #2621, #2622, #2623 (slices 1-5, all P4). Code work is tracked there.
